module_title: Aldehydes, Ketones & Carboxylic Acids: Structure, Reactivity & Preparation
introduction: This foundational level explores compounds containing the Carbonyl group ($>C=O$). Aldehydes and Ketones share similar chemical properties due to this group, while Carboxylic Acids exhibit distinct acidic behavior. Understanding the polarity of the carbonyl bond is the absolute key to mastering their reactions.

core_concepts.title: Structure and Polarity of the Carbonyl Group
core_concepts.description: The carbonyl carbon is $sp^2$ hybridized, making the $>C=O$ bond planar ($120^\circ$). Oxygen is highly electronegative, creating a strong permanent dipole ($C^{\delta+}=O^{\delta-}$). This partial positive charge on carbon acts as a powerful electrophilic center, inviting attacks from Nucleophiles. This is why the characteristic reaction of aldehydes and ketones is **Nucleophilic Addition**.

core_concepts.title: Reactivity: Aldehydes vs. Ketones
core_concepts.description:
Aldehydes are always MORE reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition due to two factors:
1. Steric Factor: Ketones have two bulky alkyl groups ($R$) that physically block the incoming nucleophile. Aldehydes have at least one small Hydrogen atom.
2. Electronic Factor: Alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I effect). The two $R$ groups in ketones push electron density toward the carbonyl carbon, reducing its positive charge ($C^{\delta+}$) and making it less attractive to nucleophiles.

core_concepts.title: General Preparation Methods
core_concepts.description:
1. Oxidation of Alcohols: Primary alcohols oxidized with PCC or Collins reagent yield Aldehydes. Secondary alcohols oxidized with $CrO_3$ or $KMnO_4$ yield Ketones.
2. Ozonolysis of Alkenes: Cleavage of $C=C$ bonds using $O_3/Zn-H_2O$ yields aldehydes or ketones depending on the substitution of the alkene.
3. Hydration of Alkynes: Ethyne reacts with $dil. H_2SO_4 / HgSO_4$ to yield Acetaldehyde. All other alkynes yield Ketones.

core_concepts.title: Introduction to Carboxylic Acids
core_concepts.description: General formula $R-COOH$. The $-COOH$ group is highly polar and can form extensive intermolecular Hydrogen bonds. In fact, most carboxylic acids exist as **Dimers** in the vapor phase and in non-polar solvents (like benzene), leading to boiling points that are significantly higher than even alcohols of comparable molecular mass.

important_entities.name: Rosenmund Reduction
important_entities.key_fact: Selective reduction of Acid Chlorides to Aldehydes.
important_entities.significance: Reaction: $R-COCl + H_2 \xrightarrow{Pd/BaSO_4} R-CHO + HCl$. The catalyst is intentionally poisoned with $BaSO_4$ (and sometimes Sulfur or Quinoline) to stop the reduction exactly at the aldehyde stage, preventing it from reducing further into a primary alcohol.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: When carbonyl compounds react with Ammonia derivatives (like $NH_2-Z$, where Z can be $-OH, -NH_2$, etc.), it is NOT just a simple addition. It is a Nucleophilic Addition followed by the Elimination of a water molecule to form a $C=N$ double bond (Imine derivatives). Example: Reacting with Hydroxylamine ($NH_2OH$) yields an Oxime ($>C=N-OH$).

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Clemmensen is Acidic (Zinc/Hg), Wolff is Basic (Wolf howls at NH2NH2)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation:
To completely strip the oxygen off a carbonyl and turn it into an alkane ($>C=O \rightarrow >CH_2$):
- **Clemmensen Reduction:** Uses Zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl ($Zn-Hg / HCl$).
- **Wolff-Kishner Reduction:** Uses Hydrazine and a strong base ($NH_2NH_2 / KOH / \Delta$). Use Clemmensen for base-sensitive molecules, and Wolff-Kishner for acid-sensitive molecules.

exam_strategy_tips: Formaldehyde ($HCHO$) is the only aldehyde that does not contain an alpha-hydrogen. Benzadehyde ($C_6H_5CHO$) also lacks an alpha-hydrogen. Keep this fact at the forefront of your mind, as it dictates whether the molecule will undergo Aldol Condensation or the Cannizzaro reaction.
